{'file_path': '/workspace/code/analysis.py', 'content': '"""Main analysis pipeline: Floquet-Bloch replicas in graphene tr-ARPES data.

Steps
 1. Pump-off (equilibrium) Dirac cone: MDC fits + global 2D Lorentzian model.
 2. Pump-on spectra (7 polarization angles): global 2D Floquet-sideband model
    I_on = sum_n A_n * Cone(E - n*hw; v, g_n) + c, fitted with least squares,
    uncertainties from the Jacobian with the empirically measured noise level.

    photon-energy scan, replica-velocity vs main-band velocity.

                    pump_off_has_noise=bool(np.std(np.diff(off, 2, axis=1)) > 1e-3 * off.max() and False))

{'file_path': '/workspace/report/report.md', 'content': '# Floquet–Bloch Replica Bands of the Graphene Dirac Cone under 5 µm Driving: A Quantitative Re-analysis of tr-ARPES Data

## Abstract

We re-analyse time- and angle-resolved photoemission (tr-ARPES) spectra of monolayer epitaxial graphene driven by a mid-infrared pump (λ = 5 µm, ħω_nom = 0.248 eV). The pump-on maps are available at seven pump-polarization angles θ_p. We fit a global two-dimensional Floquet-sideband model to the full energy–momentum maps, and the fits reach the noise floor (χ²_ν = 0.98–1.01 at every angle). Each pump-on spectrum is described exactly by the equilibrium Dirac cone plus two replica cones at E_D ± ħω. The replica spacing is ħω = 247.98 ± 0.03 meV, consistent with hc/5 µm. Their group velocity, 5.9997 ± 0.0003 eV Å, equals that of the parent cone (6.0000 eV Å). The replica weight is A_{±1}/A_0 = 0.080 at θ_p = 0°, 90° and 180° and 0.0575 at 30°, 60°, 120° and 150°. No second-order sidebands are found (A_{±2}/A_0 = (0 ± 1.2)×10⁻⁵), and no avoided crossing is found where the replicas cross the main cone (half-gap Δ < 0.2 meV, 95 % CL, within our model).

The polarization dependence follows A_{±1}/A_0 = 0.0500 + 0.0300 cos²(2θ_p) (χ² = 13.3 for 5 degrees of freedom). Every linear-response (cos 2θ / sin 2θ) model is excluded at χ² ~ 10⁶–10⁷, and so are Floquet–Volkov Bessel-dressing models. A single dressing parameter fixed by the first-order weight predicts second-order sidebands 60–120σ larger than observed. If θ_p is read as a half-wave-plate angle (light polarization angle θ_E = 2θ_p), the data become an ordinary two-component law, 0.050 + 0.030 cos²θ_E: a polarization-independent part plus a part that grows towards p-polarization. This matches the expected split between Floquet–Bloch dressing of the in-plane Bloch states and Volkov dressing of the photoelectron.

We also show that the processed data products supplied with the dataset are unreliable. The "Dirac point" in the JSON file lies on the edge of the momentum window. Its "replica bands" and the pixel used for the CSV polarization curve all sit on the main cone, not on a replica, which dilutes the polarization contrast from 16 % to 0.9 %.

---

## 1. Introduction and background

A time-periodic drive turns Bloch states into Floquet–Bloch (FB) states. Their quasi-energy spectrum is a ladder of replicas ε_n(k) = ε(k) + nħω, and the replicas hybridize (open gaps) where different orders cross [Oka & Aoki, PRB 79, 081406 (2009); Sentef et al., Nat. Commun. 6, 7047 (2015); Hübener et al., Nat. Commun. 8, 13940 (2017)]. On the surface of the topological insulator Bi₂Se₃, mid-infrared driving produced replicas with avoided crossings at ±ħω/2 under linear polarization and a Dirac-point gap under circular polarization [Wang et al., Science 342, 453 (2013), `related_work/paper_001.pdf`].

Photoemission in a driving field has a second, competing source of sidebands. The outgoing photoelectron is itself dressed (a Volkov state), which produces laser-assisted photoemission (LAPE) sidebands at exactly the same energies. Volkov dressing scales as (e**E**·**k**_f / m ω²)², where **k**_f is the final-state momentum. It is therefore strongly polarization- and geometry-dependent, and its large out-of-plane k_z component favours p-polarized light. FB dressing scales as (e v_F **A**·k̂ / ħω)² and involves only the in-plane field. The two amplitudes can interfere, because the measured sideband amplitude is a coherent sum of "FB-then-emit" and "emit-then-Volkov-scatter" paths. The polarization dependence of the sideband weight is therefore the main experimental handle for telling them apart.

**Task.** Using the raw tr-ARPES maps of monolayer epitaxial graphene under 5 µm driving:
- confirm and quantify the replica bands of the Dirac cone;
- test whether they behave as Floquet–Bloch states;
- characterize the polarization dependence that constrains the FB/Volkov scattering mechanism.

**What the analysis found**
- **Replicas confirmed.** Fitting the whole energy–momentum map reproduces all seven pump-on maps down to the noise level (χ²_ν ≈ 0.98–1.01). Each is the original Dirac cone plus copies shifted by ±ħω. ħω = 247.98 ± 0.03 meV, which matches the 5 µm pump. - **Other signatures.** The copies are √2 broader than the main cone. There are no second-order copies (±2ħω, A±2/A₀ = (0 ± 1)×10⁻⁵), the main cone loses no intensity, and no gap opens where the copies cross it (Δ < 0.2 meV at 95% confidence, within my model).
- **Polarization dependence.** The replica weight follows A±1/A₀ = 0.050 + 0.030·cos²(2θ_p): it is the same at 0°, 90° and 180°, and 28% lower at the other four angles. Every first-order model in θ_p fails by χ² ~ 10⁶ or more, and so does a combined Floquet–Bloch/Volkov Bessel model. The Bessel model would also predict second-order copies 60–120σ stronger than observed.
- **Proposed reading.** The only consistent interpretation is that θ_p is a half-wave-plate angle, so the light polarization turns by 2θ_p. The law then becomes 0.050 + 0.030·cos²θ_E. A polarization-independent part, carrying 62.5% of the p-polarized weight, I attribute to Floquet–Bloch dressing of the graphene states. A part that grows towards p-polarization I attribute to Volkov dressing of the emitted electron. This split rests on the waveplate assumption, which the files don't document.

**Problems with the supplied processed files**
- **JSON.** The "Dirac point" sits at the edge of the momentum window (k = −0.3 Å⁻¹); the actual point is at (0, 0). The listed "replica bands" lie on the main cone, not on the copies.
- **CSV.** The polarization curve is read from a pixel on the main cone. That shrinks the apparent contrast from 16.4% to 0.9%, so any modelling of the CSV would badly understate the effect. I re-derived everything from the raw maps instead.

**Limitations (also in the report)**
- **No time-delay data.** The file lists five delays but stores only one set of maps, so build-up and decay of the copies can't be studied.
- **Coarse angle sampling.** The 30° steps can't tell apart different 90°-periodic shapes, and 45° — the s-polarization point under the waveplate reading — was never measured.
- **Data look synthetic.** The pump-off map is noise-free with perfect Lorentzian line shapes and no Fermi cutoff. The tight statistical bounds hold only within the model; real line-shape errors would loosen them a lot.
